title: Developing a Strategic Negligence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article reframes a behavior that often frustrates subordinates — a leader's apparent habit of ignoring or postponing problems others consider urgent — as a deliberate and valuable skill the author calls Strategic Negligence. The claim is that the best leaders make a calculated, conscious choice about what not to address, trusting their own judgment over others' urgency claims, which frees their attention for what actually matters. The piece is careful to distinguish this from true dereliction: it only works as long as the leader stays attuned to sidelined issues and doesn't miss one that spirals out of control from inattention.
points: The behavior of ignoring or delaying problems is reframed from a leadership flaw into a named, deliberate skill — Strategic Negligence — when it's a conscious choice, not neglect.
The productivity claim is direct: each strategically postponed problem frees time and resources for what the leader has judged more important.
The article names its own failure mode explicitly: Strategic Negligence becomes dereliction the moment a leader misses a sidelined issue that spirals out of control.
quotes: As they learn the skill of delaying, postponing, abandoning, and ignoring problems others want them to prioritize, they develop a newfound insight and talent. A Strategic Negligence.
This is a calculated and deliberate choice to neglect or ignore an issue or problem while being fully aware of the risks and consequences involved.
Some of the best leaders on the planet are exceptionally skilled at ignoring issues on purpose.
In the eyes of a crafty leader at any level, each problem postponed frees up time and resources to focus on what is truly most important.
This works well as long as leaders delay the right issues and don’t miss one that will soon spiral out of control for lack of attention. That’s when Strategic Negligence becomes a dereliction.
